Soft-Tissue Wounds
 CORE
August 17, 2026
David Brogan, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Outline the reconstructive ladder.
Apply the basic principles of wound healing.
Identify common types of flaps that can be used to provide soft-tissue coverage.
Overview
Soft-tissue wounds arise in three common scenarios.
Local destruction of tissue from high-energy injury of the extremity, often accompanied by
an open fracture
Postoperative wound dehiscence, likely arising from infection or poor wound healing
secondary to intrinsic or extrinsic factors
Loss of soft tissue secondary to surgical excision of tumors or other masses




NOTES

1/22

Management of soft-tissue wounds begins with thorough débridement of all nonviable tissue.
Early involvement of a reconstructive surgeon and expedient coverage of the wound will
maximize the potential for successful limb salvage.
Physiology of Wound Healing
In general, wound healing is divided into four stages1 (Resource 1).
Hemostasis
Initial traumatic or surgical insult leads to bleeding, which is controlled by vasospasm and clot
formation.
Cytokines are released, leading to initiation of the inflammatory stage.
Inflammation
Neutrophils (0 to 48 hours postinjury), macrophages (48 to 72 hours postinjury) and
lymphocytes (>72 hours postinjury) are recruited to the wound via complex signaling cascades
to kill bacteria and prevent infection.
Persistent inflammation (because of ongoing infection) leads to a chronic wound and may
prevent healing.
Proliferation
The wound bed undergoes angiogenesis complemented by fibroblast proliferation and
formation of new extracellular matrix, followed by epithelialization and wound retraction.
Remodeling
Maturation of scar tissue and wound remodeling may occur for as long as 2 years postinjury.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Traumatic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
2/22

Traumatic injuries may include abrasions, penetrating trauma, skeletal deformation, and
degloving injuries.
Degloving injuries or Morel-Lavallée lesions represent substantial soft-tissue trauma, often
resulting in the delayed appearance of devitalized skin. This occurs secondary to injury of the
perforators that traverse the muscle and subcutaneous tissue, supplying the overlying skin.
Injury to an isolated perforator or a small group of perforators may be well tolerated because
of redundancy in perfusion of the skin.
The skin area vascularized by each perforator is referred to as an angiosome (similar to the
concept of a dermatomes in spinal innervation). Adjacent angiosomes can provide vascularity
via choke vessels in patients with a vascular injury; however, extensive destruction of
underlying perforators leads to a large avascular area that cannot be perfused via adjacent
angiosomes.
Surgical
Surgical wounds may result from poor healing of primarily closed wounds.
Iatrogenic wounds may result from surgical resection of soft-tissue tumors or débridement of
nonviable tissue secondary to trauma or infection.
Surgical wounds generally result in less trauma to the surrounding tissue; therefore, local or
regional flaps may result in a higher success rate.
Risk Factors
Risk factors for poor wound healing include systemic illness, medical comorbidities, underlying
vascular disease, use of immunosuppressant medications, diabetes mellitus, and nicotine
abuse.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients generally present with a history of trauma or postoperative infection.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
3/22

Poor wound healing secondary to loss of tissue must be distinguished from infection or poor
blood supply.
Conditions of local soft-tissue and perfusion of the limb markedly affect treatment options for
reconstructive surgery.
The quality of remaining local tissue will influence healing potential; nonviable tissue will
require aggressive débridement.
Note associated injuries, including chest-wall trauma, injury to other limbs, and possible
compromise of flap options.
Skeletal stability with well-reduced and congruent adjacent joints is a prerequisite for soft-
tissue coverage.
A well-perfused limb with a reliable blood supply also is required for attempted limb salvage,
and limb revascularization must take priority over wound management.
Neurovascular Examination
Careful neurovascular examination includes an assessment of peripheral pulses with palpation
or pencil doppler.
Note asymmetry of pulses between limbs or evidence of venous stasis changes.
The Allen test should be performed in the upper extremities to determine the patency of a
palmar arch. A patent arch allows for sacrifice of the radial artery as a donor vessel for soft-
tissue reconstruction of the upper extremity or as a potential axial vessel in flap design.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Initial evaluation should begin with radiographs to assess for skeletal deformity, which may
threaten perfusion to the surrounding soft tissue.
In patients with a chronic wound, radiographs may yield information on persistent deformity
leading to pressure sores or may identify sequelae of osteomyelitis.
Computed Tomography
CT angiography is an easily accessible option to identify vascular injuries or stenosis
contributing to tissue hypoperfusion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
4/22

Angiogram
In patients with peripheral vascular disease or prior extremity trauma, formal angiography
identifies areas of potential stenosis and may offer opportunities for endovascular
revascularization.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may aid in identifying the extent of infection in chronic wounds but has little role in the
assessment of acute injuries.
Magnetic resonance angiography has emerged as an alternative to traditional angiography,
allowing for visualization of soft tissue and vascularity in a single three-dimensional imaging
study. It can be used to identify soft-tissue injuries, such as ligament or meniscal injuries or
cartilage damage, and vascular flow, which, for certain conditions, such as knee dislocations, is
a potential advantage over traditional angiography.2 However, the low spatial resolution, cost,
limited availability, and length of examination of magnetic resonance angiography3 compared
with CT angiography limit its widespread use in preoperative planning for most patients
undergoing soft-tissue reconstruction.
Differential Diagnosis
Persistent poor wound healing often is attributed to loss of tissue, poor vascular supply, or
persistent infection. In a chronic, nonhealing wound with poor vascular supply, colonization
may lead to persistent deep infection, even if infection was not the inciting event.
Metaplastic changes of chronic wounds also can evolve into squamous cell carcinoma or other
dermatologic disorders. Biopsies of affected tissue should be considered for chronic,
nonhealing wounds.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Avoidance of wound healing complications is aided by optimizing patients before elective
surgery.
Preoperative Optimization of Patient Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
5/22

Obesity; diabetes mellitus; and the use of steroids, tobacco, and intravenous drugs are
modifiable risk factors that should be addressed, if possible, before definitive wound coverage
(Resource 2).
Optimization of a patient’s general overall health is paramount before proceeding with
coverage of chronic wounds; this may not be possible in wounds requiring acute management.
Strict avoidance of tobacco postoperatively is a modifiable risk factor that surgeons should
emphasize.

Preoperative Optimization of Patient Risk Factors
For healthy wounds without exposed vital structures, nonsurgical treatment strategies
can be attempted.
Dressing Changes
Optimal dressing for wounds is controversial. Dakin hypochlorite solution may be helpful for
infected wounds in which granulation tissue is desired.
Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy
Wound vacuum application is most helpful as a temporary measure to maintain a sterile field
between surgical procedures before definitive soft-tissue closure (Resource 3)
In some patients, wound vacuum application may be the preferred definitive method of
treatment; however, the application of wound vacuums to infected tissue may lead to
worsening infection, particularly in tissue with a marginal vascular supply. If this occurs, the
wound vacuum should be discontinued in favor of an alternative treatment strategy.

Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy
Negative-pressure wound therapy was developed as a treatment option for various
recalcitrant wounds4 and was subsequently used in combat as a temporary measure
during the Iraq war. Negative-pressure wound therapy has since proven effective in the
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
6/22

management of various civilian and combat wounds. Negative-pressure wound therapy
helps decrease wound size, maintain wound homeostasis, promote blood flow, and
remove excess fluid.5 The use of negative-pressure wound therapy in patients at risk for
bleeding because of continued anticoagulation or exposed vasculature may lead to
excessive hemorrhage. On a molecular level, negative-pressure wound therapy
upregulates expression of vascular endothelial growth factor, fibroblast growth factor,
transforming growth factor-beta, and platelet-derived growth factor. Promotion of an
anti-inflammatory wound profile leads to angiogenesis and extracellular matrix
deposition, resulting in the formation of granulation tissue.6
Surgical Management
Indications
Patients with wounds with exposed bone, devascularized tendon, evidence of ongoing
infection, or exposed hardware require surgical treatment to achieve a stable soft-tissue
envelope (Video 1).
Aggressive, early coverage of open wounds may prevent deep seeding of infection and lead to
better long-term outcomes.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
7/22

Video 1 Levin LS: Comprehensive management of soft tissue, from Patzakis MJ, mod: Open
fractures: Principles of management. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Contraindications

Contraindications
Infected wound beds are a contraindication to closure or flap coverage. Infection
increases the inflammatory response, which will be detrimental to wound healing. Flap
coverage over an infected wound will lead to prolonged deep infection if not preceded
by aggressive tissue débridement and appropriate antibiotic therapy.
Reconstructive Ladder/Elevator
Historically, reconstruction of soft-tissue defects was conceptualized as a ladder, with the
rungs representing solutions from the most basic and simple to the most complex, and the
solutions were attempted in order (Resource 4; Video 2).
Recognition of the time and effort required to proceed in order through potentially futile
reconstruction procedures has led to the concept of the reconstructive elevator, in which
surgeons may move directly to the desired procedure.7
More recently, the concept of a reconstructive supermarket has been proposed. Similar to the
manner in which a recipe requires multiple ingredients, patient care may require multiple
reconstructive techniques.8
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
8/22

Video 2 Capo JT: Surgical strategies for soft-tissue defects, from Levine WM, mod: How to raise
basic free flaps safely for orthopaedic trauma. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA, March 14-18, 2017.
Dermal Regeneration Template

Dermal Regeneration Template
Multiple regeneration templates with different compositions, both natural and synthetic,
currently are available. In general, they provide a collagen scaffold for revascularization
and neo-epithelialization to facilitate the formation of extracellular matrix and
proliferation of new tissue.9 Multiple applications have been proposed, including
coverage of exposed tendon and bone. Experience with these products may inform
appropriate use, and they should not be thought of as a substitute for healthy
vascularized tissue, particularly in areas with compromised vascular supply or a history
of infection.
Skin Graft Application
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
9/22

Split-thickness skin grafts are harvested with the use of a dermatome set to a predetermined
thickness (thin, 0.15 to 0.3 mm; intermediate, 0.3 to 0.45 mm; thick, 0.45 to 0.6 mm).
Full-thickness skin grafts may be harvested from areas of redundant tissue, usually near the
surgical field, and are closed primarily. Common sites include the inguinal crease, proximal
forearm, and medial brachium.
Healing of Skin Grafts
Imbibition—In the first 0 to 48 hours, the graft survives on diffusion of nutrients.
Inosculation—After 48 hours, vessels in the skin graft and underlying wound bed establish a
connection, and the graft becomes pink.
Revascularization—New vascular channels form within the graft in 5 to 7 days.
Local Tissue Advancement, Random Pattern Flaps, and Perforator Flaps
Random pattern flaps require harvest and advancement of skin and subcutaneous tissue
without a specific pedicle supply. Subcutaneous fat should be advanced with the tissue to
maintain the blood supply. Random pattern-flap dimensions are limited to a length to base
ratio of 2:1 to avoid a long ischemic peninsular flap.
Perforator flaps involve the use of the concept of an angiosome to aid in the surgical design of
flaps that may be elevated and used to cover adjacent soft-tissue defects or harvested as a
fasciocutaneous free flap (Video 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
10/22

Video 3 Yamashita S, Koshima I: Perforator flaps for upper limb reconstruction, from Levine WM,
mod: How to raise basic free flaps safely for orthopaedic trauma. Presented at the Annual
Meeting of the Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA, March 14-18, 2017.
Axial Pattern Flaps
Axial flaps consist of a muscle or skin with a named vessel running through the length of the
flap. Examples include gastrocnemius or soleus muscles and radial forearm flap.
Advantages include simple technique and shorter surgical time. Little postoperative
monitoring is required, and the risk of complete flap loss is low. Gastrocnemius muscle is
commonly used for coverage of the proximal third of the tibia (Video 4).
Disadvantages include the need for healthy local tissue that can be rotated into the wound;
the technique may result in additional trauma to an already-impaired extremity. If nearby
tissue is relatively ischemic secondary to trauma, prior surgery, or radiation therapy, the
likelihood of wound healing may be decreased.
SEND FEEDBACK

Video 4 Harvey EJ: Soft-tissue management: Proximal tibia, from Patzakis MJ, mod: Open
fractures: Principles of management. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, New Orleans, LA, March 6-10, 2018.
Distant Pedicled Flaps
Distant pedicled flaps require elevation of muscle or skin that remains attached to its native
blood supply to cover a distant defect. Examples include groin flap, paraumbilical perforator
flap, and cross-leg flap.
Distant pedicled flaps are associated with several advantages. Tissue may be harvested from
an area that has not been subject to trauma, radiation therapy, prior surgery, or other
potential insults to the vascular supply. Tissue also may be more supple and compliant than
that in the traumatized limb.
Disadvantages include the need for the traumatized limb to be sewn to the donor site for a
period of 3 weeks. This may be well tolerated in hand trauma that requires a groin flap for
coverage of a thumb defect but may result in digital stiffness. Cross-leg flaps require bedrest
for 3 weeks and may lead to pressure sores or deep vein thrombosis.
Free Tissue Transfer
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
12/22

Free tissue transfer may consist of skin, fascia, muscle, and/or bone harvested with its blood
supply, removed from the body, and placed into a new location within the body. The attached
blood supply is then anastomosed to recipient vessels in the new location. Examples include
free latissimus transfer, free-functioning muscle transfer, medial femoral condyle flap, or free
fibular bone flap (Videos 5 and 6).
Advantages include the ability to harvest a larger amount of tissue from a noncritical donor
site, which usually can be covered by skin graft or closed primarily. This technique provides
healthy, well-vascularized tissue to a potentially compromised area without relying on local
tissue quality. Free tissue transfer may be the only option if local soft tissue is insufficient or of
poor quality and precludes rotational flaps. The distal third of the tibia often is cited as an
example of an anatomic location with a paucity of soft tissue available for coverage purposes.
Disadvantages include a technically demanding procedure that requires sophisticated
equipment (microsurgical instruments, intraoperative microscope, microsuture) and extensive
training and expertise in microsurgery. Thrombosis within the anastomoses may lead to
catastrophic flap failure. Because of the risk for flap failure, many surgeons elect to monitor
these flaps more closely, assigning patients to a higher level of postoperative management.
Video 5 Stevanovic M: Vascularized bone grafts for limb reconstruction, from Levine WM, mod:
How to raise basic free flaps safely for orthopaedic trauma. Presented at the Annual Meeting
of the Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA, March 14-18, 2017.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
13/22

Video 6 Kasai T: Latissimus dorsi musculocutaneous flap basics to minimally invasive
techniques, from Levine WM, mod: How to raise basic free flaps safely for orthopaedic trauma.
Presented at the Annual Meeting of the Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA,
March 14-18, 2017.
Preoperative Planning

Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning for any soft-tissue coverage procedure requires a thorough
knowledge of the wound and exposed tissue at its base. If required, multiple preparatory
irrigation and débridement procedures should be performed to remove all nonviable
tissue and any potential sources of infection. Hardware may be retained if required for
sufficient skeletal fixation; however, retention of infected hardware may lead to
persistent deep infection and ultimate flap failure. The use of external fixation should be
considered, if possible, in patients with a highly contaminated or hostile wound bed.
The vascular supply to the injured limb can be assessed via a physical examination,
pencil doppler, CT angiography, or formal vascular angiography. Angiography choice is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
14/22

surgeon dependent and may be influenced by the flap type selected for coverage or
patient-specific factors.
Patient Positioning

Patient Positioning
Surgical positioning of the patient should favor the most challenging portion of the
procedure. For local flap coverage, patient positioning should facilitate rapid and safe
pedicle or perforator dissection to ensure optimal flap survival. For free tissue transfer,
the patient should be positioned to allow for easy microsurgical anastomosis, which will
ultimately determine flap survival.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Inadequate débridement and residual necrotic tissue are the most common pitfalls in the
management of soft-tissue wounds. Confidence in the reconstructive process should facilitate
aggressive débridement to remove all marginal and compromised tissue. Avoidance of
débridement because of concerns for creating a wound larger will ultimately lead to persistent
infection and undesirable outcomes.
Complications
Flap Failure

Flap Failure
Free flaps are associated with the greatest risk of flap failure, partial or complete, from
thrombosis, which usually occurs within the venous anastomosis because of the
relatively low flow system. The rate of catastrophic failure is highest within the first 24
hours postoperatively. Partial failure may be a late complication because of infection or
relative intrinsic ischemia within the flap. Complete failure of rotational flaps is relatively
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
15/22

rare but possible and usually stems from twisting of the pedicle during inset or harvest
of fasciocutaneous flaps beyond the angiosome of the identified pedicle.
Persistent Infection

Persistent Infection
Infection usually is a delayed complication, manifesting as erythema, swelling, drainage,
and pain. Incomplete wound healing or wound dehiscence for more than 4 weeks
postoperatively suggests an underlying problem, often infection or marginal necrosis of
the wound edges.
Wound Contracture

Wound Contracture
Wound contracture occurs in any wound allowed to heal via secondary intention or after
the application of dermal substitutes or skin grafts. Split-thickness grafts contract more
than full-thickness grafts, and grafting onto granulation tissue results in considerably
more contracture than grafting onto fascia. Contracture occurs because of keratinocyte
activity within the wound.10
Seroma

Seroma
Seromas form secondary to disruption of the vascular and lymphatic supply to tissue,
with a resulting increase in inflammatory factors that cause dilation of blood vessels and
increased interstitial fluid accumulation.11 Resultant dead space from flap harvest also
leads to an osmotic gradient that facilitates fluid collection. Resolution of chronic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
16/22

seromas may be a challenge to manage; therefore, prevention of seromas via adequate
drainage of the flap donor site is imperative, with drains routinely left in place for as long
as 2 weeks postoperatively.
Hematoma

Hematoma
Meticulous hemostasis must be achieved before wound closure to prevent hematoma
collection, which leads to wound breakdown and infection. Passive drains often are left
in place beneath flaps after free tissue transfer to minimize hematoma formation.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Recognition of preoperative nerve palsy in the injured limb is important, because
patients with a mangled limb and soft-tissue deficits often may have associated sensory
and/or motor nerve loss at the time of injury. Careful dissection of recipient
vessels/pedicles, which may have nearby associated nerves, avoids additional neural
injury to the traumatized limb. Some sensory loss may be unavoidable in the harvest of
fasciocutaneous flaps, and patients should be counseled preoperatively about this
possibility.
New Onset Vascular Insufficiency

New Onset Vascular Insufficiency
Rarely, in patients with a highly traumatized limb, additional attempts at soft-tissue
coverage from local tissue rearrangement may lead to additional vascular
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
17/22

embarrassment. Careful preoperative assessment may help to identify limbs at risk,
particularly those with a history of vascular injury or insufficiency. Surgeons must
consider whether attempts at limb salvage are warranted in these patients.
Postoperative Management
Primary Closure

Primary Closure
Dressings remain in place for 5 days and are changed daily thereafter until sutures are
removed.
Wound Vacuums

Wound Vacuums
Wound vacuums are changed weekly (at a minimum) and are monitored for signs of
worsening infection. If the wound is malodorous, repeat irrigation and débridement is
performed, dressings are soaked with Dakin solution, or an antibiotic bead pouch is
initiated.
Rotational Flaps

Rotational Flaps
The affected limb is elevated for 5 days postoperatively, with skin graft dressings left in
place throughout this period. Nicotine is avoided until the wound has healed. Skin graft
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
18/22

dressings are changed 5 days postoperatively; the limb may be dependent at this time;
however, judicious use of soft, compressive dressings is imperative to manage swelling.
Free Flaps
Flap Diet

Flap Diet
After free tissue transfer, patients should not eat or drink for 24 hours postoperatively to
allow for emergent flap revision/thrombectomy if necessary. After 24 hours
postopertively, a regular diet is advanced; however, nicotine, caffeine, and chocolate are
prohibited for 6 weeks to minimize the risk of flap ischemia.
Activity

Activity
Patients with a lower extremity free flap should remain on strict bedrest for 5 days
postoperatively given the potential risk for intravascular thrombosis. A convective
temperature management system is applied to the extremity to maximize peripheral
vasodilation and blood flow. All patients with a lower-extremity flap should remain non–
weight bearing until clear signs of healing are observed (usually 2 to 3 weeks
postoperatively or longer if necessary).
Dangling Protocol

Dangling Protocol
To minimize venous congestion, extremities with free flaps are elevated for 7 days
postoperatively, after which they are allowed to dangle for 15 minutes every 2 hours.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:38 AM
AAOS | Soft-Tissue Wounds
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002050
19/22

This is advanced by 15 minutes every week for 1 month, at which point the restrictions
are lifted.
Outcomes
Successful management of soft-tissue injuries depends on various local and patient-related
factors.
The likelihood of successful wound healing is high if the patient is kept in a clean bed and has
an adequate amount of well-vascularized tissue; however, if these criteria are not met, wounds
may continue to be problematic for a prolonged period.
Success rates of free tissue transfer are higher than 90%, with little difference between muscle
and fasciocutaneous flaps.12,13 Early involvement of a reconstructive microsurgeon will yield
optimal results, facilitating a comprehensive strategy for wound débridement, skeletal fixation,
and robust soft-tissue coverage. The optimal reconstructive strategy for a patient will be based
on the surgeon’s experience and technical abilities, patient comorbidities, and wound
characteristics.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Débride the wound aggressively and remove hardware, if possible, to eliminate sources of
persistent infection.
Flaps will not cure infections but may prevent secondary infection by providing coverage of a
clean wound.
Efforts should be made to manage the underlying problem that caused the initial wound (eg,
infection, poor vascular supply, necrotic tissue secondary to radiation therapy). Failure to
recognize these problems will result in persistent lack of wound healing.
Mark as Complete
